utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Please be seated. Yesterday I asked for some research and investigation, but unfortunately we didn't find any letter related to the following witness. I would, therefore, ask the Defence to present this missing letter accompanied by the proof of your fax machine that it was sent before today, no later than 7 January 2003. And also, as a result of the reflections on the statements and proffers on the witnesses in the past, it is not only the Prosecution but, first of all, the Prosecution, also the Chamber that sometimes take the liberty to go into the merits and to try to find out who the person is that is called. We did it in the past related to witnesses of the Prosecution, and we'll do it in the future related to witnesses of the Defence. And if only one date, for example, February 2 related to February 3, it confuses everything, and we are not able to do the work necessary for our preparation. Enough of preliminary remarks. I can't see any movement of the parties. Therefore, let us hear our witness today. Nothing has changed, and the witness is still to be heard in public without any protective measures. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do have an issue, Your Honour, if I may with all due respect. My office is actually in Chicago, so we will endeavour to find the letter. Yesterday, the Court identified a letter which identified Witness Q and there were some comments made from the OTP with respect to that letter, and then my insistence that a second letter was sent. For the record, ultimately, that second letter was retrieved in Ms. Joanna Korner's office, on her desk. I subsequently called my office and received the fax confirmation for those two letters, which I have now. I do not have an extra copy, but the Court's welcome to take this one. So as long as I get a copy from the Court Registrar. So those are the two letters that were sent on those dates. I also, just for the record, want to state that I spoke with Ms. Korner last Friday actually on two occasions at approximately 3.00, and also at 6.00 later that evening, in connection with both Witness Q and the upcoming witness. It's my firm belief, despite the fact that Ms. Joanne Korner is not here that she will indeed recall those conversations because they, in fact, did occur. The facsimiles were sent, for example, the second letter which the Court did not receive, there are specific instructions to Mr. Christian Rohde whom we in every occasion have faxed our briefs, our motions et cetera, and asked that they be distributed to the appropriate parties. Within that cover sheet statement, we direct him to distribute that second letter to the respective Trial Chambers and Your Honours. I'll tender that with the Court's permission to the usher. But then again I must have another copy in Chicago, but this is the only one I have here so I don't have a courtesy copy for the OTP this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it from this that the two letters we have before us from you dated December 4, 2002, they were sent by fax, but there was no additional letter, no letter related to the witness we called today. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just not sure. I'm going to have to go back and check that with my office. They were unable to find it last night. I have a specific recollection because I wrote the letters that we split them in this fashion. As I indicated to the Court yesterday in our 65 ter conference, I'm going to have to personally make that inquiry. But as of right now, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it remains with what I said earlier, we expect this letter and the fax proof that it was sent no later than 7 of January. Thank you. May there -- being no other issues, would you please be so kind and escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Murselovic. Mr. Murselovic, we all know that you testified before this Trial Chamber already in May this year. This Tribunal consists of three columns: The Prosecution, registry, Chambers, and then we have the Defence. I don't want to go into further details. Due to unfortunate reasons, we had to ask you to come once again and answer the one or other question. I hope it will be a relatively short exercise. But on behalf of the Tribunal, I apologise for any inconvenience emanating from this. As to the fact that it's a new testimony, would you be kind enough to once again give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court wanted to be reminded. We didn't formally call the case yet this morning. I don't know that it's necessary, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary, and I explicitly thank you. Would you please -- maybe it's interesting also for the witness to know in which case he makes his statement today, that he is not confused at all, being one day here, the next day there. Would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And it should also be reflected from the transcript who appears. May I ask you, thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Kapila Waidyaratne, Nicholas Koumjian, and Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecution. If I can just add one brief comment, I did speak to Ms. Korner last night, and she did confirm that she had a conversation about the witnesses with Mr. Ostojic. I don't have all the details, but she did confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I also, for the record, have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: John Ostojic on behalf of Dr. Milomir Stakic, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So as to the fact that it is the witness of the Prosecution and we have reopened the Prosecution's case for this special purpose, the first word is, of course, for the Prosecution, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then formally, for the Defence. And please, as advised yesterday, tell us on what concrete statement. You need not name it, but tell us the number and the page number that we know on which part of the new statements this is based.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Just if I may with the Court's permission introduce myself. My name is John Ostojic. I represent Dr. Stakic here. On behalf of the Defence, I want to thank you for scheduling time to meet with us and possibly discuss some issues in this case. In advance, I'd like to thank you for your time and your testimony and also apologise for any inconvenience that may have caused you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first issue that the Defence would like to inquire on is with respect to Witness 1185, and specifically the background, as the Court knows, it was not known to the Defence that this witness also was in the same background and profession as Witness Number 85 [sic]. In light of that, not having Witness Number 115's [sic] statement, we would like to ask this witness to the extent if he had any profession dealings with Witness Number 1185. I'm not certain how we're going to proceed unless the witness knows who Witness Number 1185 really is without identifying him. But I'll be happy to proceed in the manner the Court suggests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until now, the Defence has been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- Find their own way. Please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the witness is not protected, correct, Your Honour? So I may use his name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you were in the catering business in 1992 and before. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, during this time period, know or are you familiar with the fact that Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic was also in the catering business at or around that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic was never in catering. He was a mathematics teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if a gentleman by the name of Mr. Simo Miskovic was involved in the catering business at all?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Simo Miskovic worked in the police. He was a policeman, and he retired from the police. I don't know what he did once he was retired, but he went into retirement from the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... That you did not know that Mr. Simo Miskovic was in the catering business and had a restaurant or a cafe in Prijedor or in the municipality of Prijedor in 1992 or prior to that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't do that professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know Mr. Simo Miskovic and Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Kuruzovic because we both worked at the same school for one period of time. I also worked there as a maths teacher. But I also knew him from town, because he sometimes came to my restaurant. I knew him from the street. He is a native of Prijedor. And that's how I also knew him. I knew where he resided as a child. There was a house in front of the municipality building. That's where he lived. That was then pulled to the ground, and then he moved to Puharska, to another part of the town. So I can say that I knew him rather well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to the events that unfolded in the spring and summer of 1992, would you consider yourself to be a friend, a social acquaintance, or merely someone who knew about either Simo Miskovic and/or Slobodan Kuruzovic? How would you categorise your relationship?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that we were acquaintances. I knew him. We would say hello to each other when we bumped into each other. But we were not friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you know of the fact that in 1992, Mr. Kuruzovic lost his young daughter, she died, in Sarajevo? Did you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt this. I do not see any relevance with regard to this line of questioning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it might establish the extent of his relationship possibly with Mr. Kuruzovic. And this is the information, the first time the Defence has learned it from the disclosures. If the Court would like, I could direct your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you find a bridge or case immediately we would allow one further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is the witness permitted to answer this question or not, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: He is permitted to answer this question, but then, please, find the bridge to our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just reminded me about the fact that Mr. Kuruzovic lost his young daughter immediately prior to the beginning of the war. But how did -- how that happened, what were the circumstances of that event, I don't know. We were not so close, and I didn't even go to that funeral. I just heard that as information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Couple of other areas specifically relating to the Red Cross and a stay in Omarska, that being submitted during the disclosure on Rule 68. I don't have my notes with the transcript page. It is of a witness which the Court has. I don't have the number in front of me. Perhaps in private session, I can identify it for the Court. I think the witness clearly in his statement said that he was a member of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know what you are speaking about. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, are you familiar with and were you acquainted with a gentleman by the name of Srdjo Srdic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know, did you have in information in the spring and summer, what Mr. Srdjo Srdic's job and function were of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srdjo Srdic is also a native of Prijedor. He is an elderly man who was a dentist. I knew his parents. And he was a frequent patron of my restaurant. He worked in the medical centre as a dentist, and he worked in the so-called Celuloza. That's what we called those premises. He was my very frequent patron, and I knew him better than the previous two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information or belief that after leaving the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Srdic served as president of the Red Cross in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that after we had been taken to the camp, that he was the president of the Red Cross and that he was in charge of issuing permits for those who wanted to leave Prijedor Municipality. But while I was in Prijedor, I believe that he wasn't the president of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure, and I don't want to give you something that is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They in this Tribunal say if I may with the Court's permission, my case to you with respect to this issue, Mr. Srdic, if he were to claim that he was the president of the Red Cross, and that he visited Omarska on a regular basis and provided medical care, treatment, utilities, and facilities to those that required it, wouldn't that be the truth, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. The Defence is abusing their rights absolutely. It was clearly stated yesterday that the line of questions should be limited to those not available at that time when the witness appeared. You're making reference to a statement of August 2002. This is the first point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with what the Court's referring to, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You should listen to what is said in the courtroom. And second, there were objections to the concrete questions by the Prosecution. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, the objection is I don't believe -- I believe counsel has made an error, and I don't believe he has a good faith belief that he will present evidence that Mr. Srdic visited the camp every day. Because I think the transcript will show that, in fact, there's a denial that he ever visited the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And as we stated yesterday, reference should be made to the concrete passage of the five interviews or statements not available at that time when we heard the witness before us for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you can make reference to the concrete page that we can be sure that you don't quote just out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On page 2699 of Mr. Murselovic's previous testimony, let me back up just a bit here. If I can just be corrected, on page 2815 of Mr. Murselovic's testimony, I'd like to ask him further about who the most prominent politicians were. He identifies specifically in that transcript several individuals, and then concludes in that narrative that he considered, I'm reading from my notes here, the first three to be the most powerful politicians in Prijedor. I'd like to ask him a couple questions relating to that question as well as the question on Crisis Staff, and I'd like to ask him questions specifically about two other individuals whose disclosures we received pursuant to Rule 68, Vojo Pavicic, and Ranko Travar. Specifically, we would to ask him questions with respect to Mr. Pavicic on page 7, lines 1 through 4 of his interview. If this gentleman being a former member of the Municipal Assembly in view of what Mr. Travar's function was, to determine whether Mr. Murselovic knew that Mr. Travar was a member of the Crisis Staff. We would like to put to the witness, if permitted by the Court pursuant to the Rules of this Tribunal, our case, since Mr. Pavicic clearly on pages 15 and 16 of his interview, lines 20 through 32, page 15 of his interview, page 16, lines 19 through 25, page 19, lines 14 through 16; page 21, lines 13 through 16, discusses who was present and who was not during some of the Crisis Staff meetings. This, we believe, will relate specifically to the testimony given by Mr. Murselovic from pages 2699 when he gives an opinion about the synchronisation and coordination of the Crisis Staff between various institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. But we were still discussing the question of Mr. Srdjo Srdic, as you stated, regular visits in his capacity of president of the Red Cross in Omarska. And I didn't find something like this, but please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The question was indeed awkward. I think if the Court can see from page 2722 of Mr. Srdic's testimony, which was disclosed pursuant to Rule 68 -- I apologise. I'm giving the Court an incorrect page number. The sum and substance of Mr. Srdic's testimony as president of the Red Cross was that the Red Cross was present, I believe, at -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Should I just suggest that we go into private session when we are talking about matters that were not -- were perhaps deemed confidential by individuals at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. We received a number of documents apparently from the Defence. Do you want to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: These documents, Your Honour, relate to the issue that arose yesterday with respect to whether or not a facsimile and letters were sent to Ms. Joanna Korner, and to the individual I mentioned this morning, Mr. Christian Rohde, regarding the response to the OTP's letter of December 3rd and December 4th respectively. I think if the Court -- or as the Court knows, looking at the last two pages of the bundle that was received, this is a confirmation sheet, or as we call it a confirmation sheet that the faxes which were sent, the pages indicated below, were, indeed, received. And it is our position that that was our duty, simply to get a confirmation. Simply the result indicating okay is my understanding a confirmation that it was received. And as the Court will look on the second page of the document, as we have in the past when communicating with the Court, we directed the letter to Mr. Christian Rohde at the facsimile letter that was available to us in the past. And specifically state that in that facsimile cover sheet that he "kindly forward the attached letter to the Trial Chamber as indicated." It was our impression that the Court did receive or the Court should have received it. We were obviously misguided. We didn't know the Court had not received it. In the past, when we sent communications, whether it was a motion or a request, we operated under this procedure and we seem to have met some success. I'm not certain why in this particular time, the OTP didn't receive our second response, also dated December 4th, and why the Court did not receive both our responses to those letters. So we apologise for that, but we will try to establish a new procedure to confirm that any correspondence is received before we appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's now not no longer disputed, and this was already yesterday the case, that there were two letters apparently, one related to Witness Q and one related to witnesses in -- I don't know. They are not protected. Nusret Sivac and Mirza Mujadzic, and nothing was mentioned in this letter related to Mr. Muharem Murselovic. This is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. But I can also for the record with the Court area permission identify that in my conversation with Ms. Joanna Korner on Friday of last week confirmed to her orally that we would withdraw our request with respect to Witness Q and that we would also be seeking leave to question Mr. Murselovic upon his arrival to The Hague. It's my understanding that Mr. Murselovic testified in this case for longer than a couple sessions. And having known that he was going to testify on the 11th, namely yesterday, on the Brdjanin case, we were not advised when he would be available in the Stakic case. I would ask if the Court permits that the OTP specifically -- or if they can, advise us when Mr. Mujadzic is coming, because we would like to put several questions to him that stem from the transcript of specifically three individuals since those three individuals and those interviews specifically mention Mr. Mujadzic. And we would like to at least put our case to him in connection with those conversations and facts as we've described this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In order to have the transcript correct, it should be emphasised that in the letter from the OTP also addressed to the Trial Chamber, we were informed that Mr. Murselovic would be in The Hague from the 9th of December and testify on 11 December. There was nothing ambiguous in this. And it is not to discuss among the parties an upcoming witness. If you want to hear and want to call a witness, please inform the Court, because it's the Court that has to decide whether or not the threshold has been met or not. Coming now to our witness, what is the estimated time you believe to need for concluding? And please, don't misinterpret this as an invitation to be short, because apparently we need some more details on the personality of Dr. Stakic. What is the estimated time you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Approximately an hour to an hour and a half, Your Honour, but it's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll spend as much time with him as I believe necessary and the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then what would be the remaining witnesses for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The remaining witnesses for this week would be one after Mr. Makovski, and that would be Mr. Mico Kos, as we have identified previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Didn't you ask for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we did, Your Honour, we are withdrawing that orally since I spoke to Mr. Kos, and we were not going to seek protective measures for his testimony when he testifies. So to the extent that we did, it was clarified with the witness, and he did not require any such protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the name need not be redacted from the transcript today. And it's my understanding that you want to prepare the examination-in-chief. And therefore hear this witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be the Defence's request, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it would finally allow the Judges to participate in the second occupation of the day, to participate in the plenary. And therefore we agree. And hear the second witness. May I ask, what about Witness 068?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That witness, the Defence is withdrawing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally. Definitively?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about 71?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 71, Your Honour, is not able to appear this week, is not in The Hague. And we expect to call 71 in the first two weeks of January. I know we've provided the OTP and the Court with a list. We can also call him immediately following those witnesses on the list in order that there be no confusion. So we can call him at some time later, possibly after those next ten witnesses or so that we have identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We don't have any problems at all as we are prepared to hear this witness already now, in the framework of the list you have given to us, so it's no problem at all to hear this witness in addition to the other persons mentioned in this list. So therefore, we would invite you, if possible, to call this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are two other matters when the Court allows that I would like to address with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One is personal and a sensitive issue if I may that we are asking the Court's assistance and intervention if you will. I checked with the -- my learned friend from the Office of the Prosecution. After this witness testifies, Your Honour, we would like, if the Court permits, for him to be able to meet with Dr. Stakic. Dr. Stakic specifically has requested that. That approval to meet with this witness at the Detention Centre, because of the procedures and delay in doing what I think their security background checks, they say that they would not allow him access to the Detention Centre. If this Court permits, and if there is obviously no objection from the OTP, we would ask if the Court can allow this witness to meet with Dr. Stakic for no more than 20 to 30 minutes, but certainly no more than 30, in the presence of the security staff and, with the Court's, Chamber's, their staff if necessary, just so that we can exchange pleasantries and say hello to each other. Both have requested that, both Mr. Makovski and Dr. Stakic. And I am formally making that application, having spoken with the OTP briefly earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should know anyhow how -- how difficult this is to arrange this through OLAD and the acting Dutch authorities at the same time. So wouldn't it be - we have to decide on this, no doubt - a better environment to have this meeting, if we agree, here in the premises of the ICTY instead of the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is what I'm suggesting. I'm sorry, Your Honour. That they meet here immediately following the testimony of Mr. Makovski, with your permission, in the back Chamber there or whatever the Court allows with anyone present that the Court allows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, we don't object from the interests of the Prosecution, but we are not seeking to interfere with whatever decisions the security and OLAD, whatever procedures they have. But it does not prejudice -- we do not see any prejudice to our own case if following his testimony they meet. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9749 to 9754.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We rule on this after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And my final application, and thank you, Your Honour, is that several months ago we requested that the Defence have January 7th off because of the Serbian orthodox Christmas, and the Court was kind of enough to grant that to us. For a practical matter that we did not envision, bringing witnesses to The Hague, because we start on the 8th of January, would require us to bring them and actually have them depart either on the 6th or the 7th. And I believe -- at least my request and the Court's granting of the request to have the 7th off, we're trying to arrange for, if I can say respectfully, for non-Serbian Orthodox witnesses to come that three days remaining in that week. The list doesn't reflect that, but we're working through that. I noticed that actually last night and wanted to raise it with the Court. To the extent that we can, we will advise the Court and the OTP immediately of that schedule. Some of the witnesses will not or would be hesitant to appear, having to be taken away in the middle of a holiday from their families during that January 7th period. Again, just so the record is clear, this is an error from a practical sense that the Defence made. We should have perhaps envisioned this, and the Court did grant us the 7th, and we do appreciate that. We're just working through trying to find a solution because the witness and victim and protection unit would have to bring these witnesses at least a day or two prior to their testimony, which would then interfere with their personal holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We had the same problem last year. And the position taken by the bureau at that time was that we have to stick to the holidays of the United Nations, being an institution of the United Nations. Therefore, it was already an exception not really respected by other judges as the correct approach that we decided to grant the 6th and the 7th. As the Court calendar reads, the trials have to start the 6th. And we can't wait only one day longer. Therefore, unfortunately, being faced already with problems emanating from the fact that we granted two additional days, we can't grant any more days. Sorry for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we ask now that Mr. Makovski be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Makovski. Our apologies that apparently you had to wait a longer time than expected. But fortunately, we can now proceed with your testimony. And let's start immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Makovski, good morning, I'm going to continue to ask some questions in connection with the relationship that you had with Milomir Stakic and his family. Yesterday you shared with us some insights with respect to that relationship. I'm going to try to put some questions to you so we can all better understand and appreciate Dr. Milomir Stakic. And you being more than an acquaintance with him, you, sir, hopefully can assist us in having a complete understanding of Dr. Stakic. I apologise if I interrupt. It's not an attempt to be rude or to not allow you to have an opportunity to fully and completely share with us your views, your opinions, and your observations of Dr. Stakic. However, at times, the Defence, as well as perhaps our learned friends from the OTP and the Honourable Court, would like some further insights into those meetings and developing relationships that you have of Dr. Stakic. So if I may, sir, do you consider and did you consider Dr. Stakic as a friend?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During his youth, did you, sir, at any time observe whether or not Dr. Stakic was a violent person?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, he was no different really from the other children. He was not a violent person. He was not one of the leaders, either, although, perhaps, because he was exceptionally intelligent, he deserved to be one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you describe Dr. Stakic as a nonviolent person; and if so, explain why?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as children play, there is usually contact between the children. And he never returned any blows or any shoves that he received. And whenever he was on the receiving end, he never complained. He never told tales to his parents or the teacher. Even if most pupils tend to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And staying with the time period of Dr. Stakic's youth, did you feel you knew him enough in order to make an assessment at that time of his character?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him definitely well enough to be able to judge his character and nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Explain to us, if you will, sir, in your opinion, the character of Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic is a silent, peaceful man who doesn't like to impose on other people. I knew him when he was growing up. He is a family-loving man. He respects and values other people and would never harm anyone on any account.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so we can get an appreciation of the times that you saw Dr. Stakic as a youth, would you say that it was on a daily and regular basis? Did you see him often during his youth?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis, I should say. It was his -- the education he received at home which then continued at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time, sir, see or observe Dr. Stakic making discriminatory remarks against any non-Serbs, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, by no means. He loved me exceptionally well. He almost adored me. Not only did he love me, but also his parents. Not his parents, the entire village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned on page 42, line 10, that Dr. Stakic, among other things, was a peaceful man. Can you share with us what you mean by that and the basis for that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a silent person, the sort of person who wouldn't impose on other people in any way. As a boy, he never wanted to be in the forefront. He never wanted to be very prominent. He even helped perhaps less talented pupils to master all the lessons at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, Dr. Stakic's character at that time. And I know you highlighted it briefly for us yesterday, with respect to women during the time period of his youth. What I'm looking for, Mr. Makovski, if I may, is to determine whether or not he exhibited any signs of violence against women, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was a boy, they all played together in one group, boys and girls, there was no difference. But he never displayed any violent attitude to boys or to girls, for that matter. Later, I spent time with him when he was already an adult, a married man. I already said that even the nurses working at the medical sector, all the lady doctors held him in high esteem. Not only did they hold him in high esteem, they had respect for him. I observed that their relationship was very often playful. They told each other jokes, and their relationship was just normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, you were able to reach that conclusion based upon your personal experiences and contacts with these nurses working at the medical sector. Correct? And these lady doctors, as you identify; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used to go there very often to his office, and I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you can, your opinion in connection with Dr. Stakic relating to his morality and decency?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic's morality was spotless, impeccable. It was a very high level of personal ethics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may move to the time period of the spring and summer of 1992, did you know, sir, in the spring and summer of 1992, that Dr. Stakic was initially vice-president of the Municipal Assembly in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you also subsequent to that, sir, learn that after April 30th, 1992, Dr. Stakic purportedly was president of the Municipal Assembly of the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At that time, sir, can you share with us what your thoughts were with respect to Dr. Stakic's personality being placed in that function? And sir, what I'm looking for is to have you make an assessment, if you can, based on your personal observations of Dr. Stakic whether he was a man who for that position had a lack of experience and was naive possibly, and as I think you mentioned, would at times and could be subject to being manipulated. Can you share that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic had a very uneasy position in politics. He didn't really seem to be finding his way around with much ease. Because in politics, a different set of rules applies. It's the homo homini lupus sort of thing in politics. Or to use the boxer's jargon, there are plenty of punches below the belt in that environment. And often people didn't choose really -- they weren't choosy about their means to attain their ends. But Dr. Stakic was a man who loved and appreciated other people. And he never wanted to harm anyone, not by his action, not by his words. That is why he was not really at ease in politics, I think. I believe that other people may have used this, his human kindness, to simply manipulate him as a human being, as a young human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to philanthropy, charity, and humanitarianism, do you, sir, have an opinion of those issues on the character and reputation of Dr. Stakic? And share with us any insights you may have in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, in simply terms, should have, and I believe he did it later, stayed in his job. He should have dedicated his life to medicine. It's a shame that he spent one part of his life in politics. If he hadn't, he would have done so much more in the medical science. I believe that he would be, and I still leave that he will still be a top-class doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Knowing Dr. Stakic as you did, and do, could you ever envision a situation or a circumstance in which Dr. Stakic would aid or assist in committing a crime against women and children?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he could have never done something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the way he is, his personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Could you ever envision Dr. Stakic committing a crime against any individual, men, women or children?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Could you envision a situation, sir, having known Dr. Stakic as long as you have, of Dr. Stakic ordering a third party to commit a crime against any individuals, including men, women, or children?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply cannot imagine any such thing. At that time, I never heard anybody uttering a bad -- a single bad word about Dr. Stakic. Had I heard anybody saying a bad word about him, or saying that he had done something bad, believe me, I wouldn't be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Following up on that answer, then, sir, I have a two-part question. First, is it true that at no time during the spring and summer of 1992 did you hear Dr. Stakic or were told by any individuals that Dr. Stakic made discriminatory remarks that would be deemed to be intimidating non-Serbs, including Muslims and Croats, among others?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something: At that time, I couldn't follow the media. There was no electricity. Whatever I could hear, I heard from neighbours who were standing in front of my house, on the street, at school. But I never heard anything bad about Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday, and I apologise I don't have the transcript yet, and I'll try to paraphrase it, that you met Dr. Stakic again in 1992, and that you embraced when he saw you while you were with your wife, and that he identified you as his "dear teacher," I believe. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that as if had happened yesterday. I have very fond memories of that meeting, and that was approximately sometime in mid-July. It was summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's my question to you first: Do you remember when this meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting occurred in the afternoon in mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sometime in July of 1992. Can you tell us where you encountered and saw Dr. Stakic in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had met him at the Oskar cafe-bar, or at Kod Pale as they call it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Question, but I think it's clear and I mean no disrespect to you, we have used from time to time categorisation of ethnic backgrounds. I know you don't consider yourself -- let me ask the question. You are not a Serb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again with my deepest respect, can I clarify for the purposes of my couple questions, you are a non-Serb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At that meeting in July of 1992, to the best of your recollection, were other Serbs in this cafe, other than Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was in the cafe. I didn't pay attention to them. When the doctor approached me, I felt a certain warmth, and I couldn't see anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... On the part of Dr. Stakic to come towards you and to embrace you, despite the fact, and again, with the deepest respect, you are a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miso was the one who saw me first. I didn't see him. He was the one who saw me. I have been brought up not to look at other people's tables to see what they are eating or drinking. He was the one who saw me first and rushed towards me. Absolutely irrespective of the fact whether I was a Serb or a Croat or a Bosniak, that was not important. In my head, it never existed, and I also believe that it never existed in the mind of Miso.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it wasn't translated because I didn't allow you to conclude your answer. But the question on line -- I'm sorry. Perhaps it wasn't translated because I didn't allow you to conclude your previous answer. But my question on line 15 should have started: "Did Dr. Stakic hesitate, or did you see any hesitancy on the part of Dr. Stakic in coming towards you, a non-Serb?" In July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat once again. I didn't see Dr. Stakic sitting at the table. It was he who saw me. I also didn't see other people sitting at the table. I have been brought up not to look at people's dining tables to see what they are eating or drinking. I wasn't interested in that. But the doctor saw me, rushed towards me. I think that he was so glad to see me, as if I was his own father.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think the problem is that counsel is asking his question before the interpretation. That's why the transcript can't keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me whether he hesitated, Dr. Stakic. No, not for a single moment did Dr. Stakic hesitate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In July of 1992, during this visit, did Dr. Stakic hesitate in any manner whatsoever to embrace you, a non-Serb, in a public meeting place?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't hesitate. He embraced me first and took me by surprise. Then I was all of a sudden seized by a warmth, and there was a surge of emotions. I was glad that after such a long time, I saw a former child whom I really liked before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time during this conversation and meeting that you had with Dr. Stakic in the public restaurant in July of 1992, did Dr. Stakic exhibit any signs of nervousness, a cold attitude, or indifference towards you, a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. On the contrary. He was smiling; he was all smiles. He was happy, joyful. He behaved as somebody who spots a dear friend whom he hadn't seen in a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, sir, the respect that Dr. Stakic had and has for your wife.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I first came to Dr. Stakic's apartment with my wife, he didn't know my wife. But his wife knew my wife because the two of them are natives of the same village. He was a gentleman, and he behaved as one. He pulled a chair for my wife and asked her to take a seat first. To my mind, this is a sign of good manners, and this portrayed him as a gentleman in my eyes. In his speech, he didn't use any bad or indecent words that men sometimes use when they talk to each other. He chose his words very carefully, making sure that all of these words were polite.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to ask a leading question. However, you shared with me, sir, a couple days ago an experience that you were starting to tell us about your wife. And you also mentioned, just to refresh your recollection, that your wife is considerably younger than you are. Can you share with us the respect that Dr. Stakic had to your wife, to a man who's a non-Serb, to a younger woman perhaps closer to the age of Dr. Stakic? And I'm only trying to refresh your recollection in connection with that which you shared with me previously.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My wife is 12 years younger than me. She is a very pretty woman, I should say. She is Serbian. She was born in a -- in a village called Busnovi, the same village where Miso's wife was born. I used to work in that village school for 15 years teaching older children. I was an assistant chief administrator of the school, the principal of that school, and the villagers of that village held me in high esteem. They respected me, although I'm not a Serb. I never experienced, in all the 35 years of my work, somebody putting me down or belittling me because I am not a Serb. On the contrary, everybody respected me and held me in high esteem. And although I came with my wife at that time, every man tends to display a certain degree of lustful feelings towards good-looking women. You can see it in their eyes. But in Miso's eyes, I didn't see any signs of that. He respected me, and therefore, he respected my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, at any time did Dr. Stakic or anyone tell you that Dr. Stakic was seeking to be a part of a plan to make an ethnically pure municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've already told you, in 1992, I met him. We exchanged a few words. And the next time I saw him was in 1994 when I sought him out to ask for medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a moment, I hope. Help me to understand Dr. Stakic not only as a student that you've just done but also as the son, while you interchanged with his parents. Describe for us, if you will, his relationship with his parents, specifically that which you've observed.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: His relationship with his parents was exceptional. He was tender towards them. He was very loyal to his family. While he was a student of medicine in Banja Luka, he would spend every free moment that he had with his family, unlike most of the youngsters who tend to go out to socialise with other young people of their age, with girls. Instead of that, he would go to his native village to see his parents. He helped them with heavy farmwork. And I'm sure you will recognise that very few young people, adolescents, that is, will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Staying with this period and your observations of Dr. Stakic as the son, in describing for us that, did you notice at any time Dr. Stakic exhibiting any disrespect, anger, or hatred towards his parents?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've just told you is based on what I heard from his cousin in Banja Luka in 1994. It was when Miso sent me there for some medical tests. I had developed a heart condition, so he sent me to a test called ergometry. A nurse -- the nurse who worked there was his relative. While we were chatting, the two of us, by accident, I happened to mention to her that it was Miso who had referred me for this test. And then she told me about him and the way he was as a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... At any time tell you that Dr. Stakic was disrespectful or exhibited any anger towards them as parents? Did they ever complain to you or tell you and share with you the type of son Dr. Stakic was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Not his mother, Mira, not his father, Milan. They never complained, not in a single word, against their son. They both loved him from the bottom of their hearts, and he returned their love and respect with equal measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may ask you to focus on the relationship Dr. Stakic had with his children, I believe your testimony yesterday was that you were able to personally observe that relationship. So now describe for us, please, Dr. Stakic as a father.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in his apartment several times, and I didn't notice him using harsh words in communication with his children. On the contrary. He was very tender. Not only towards his children, but also towards his wife, whom he respected and still respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You anticipated my next question. In addition, I wanted to ask about the relationship of Dr. Stakic as a husband. Did likewise his wife share the same respect towards Dr. Stakic as he did towards her? Or to the best of your ability, describe their relationship, that which you've personally observed.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was mutual trust and respect in that relationship. They cared about each other. They loved each other. And most importantly, for a family to be happy, that is the most important thing. Also, for their children's happiness. One of the reasons may be that he himself had grown up in such a family where the wife, the mother, was deeply respected and where children were loved. So he continued down the same path with his own family.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'm going to ask you, Mr. Makovski, can you share with us your reaction when you heard that Dr. Stakic was detained and arrested and brought to The Hague. What was your reaction, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cried. Even now, whenever I think back to that, tears swell in my eyes. A man like him, a son like Dr. Stakic, a parent, a father like him, a husband like him, exceptionally honest, a diligent, hard-working man, to be arrested as a war criminal, I took a long time to pull myself back together. My emotions were, how should I put it, my emotions, my feelings for that man, I don't think I can put this into words right now. I can't find the right words, how difficult it was for me, how bad I felt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can change the subject a little, and then with the Court's permission, we'll come back to this issue and others with respect to Dr. Stakic's character and reputation, if necessary. Sir, in the spring and summer of 1992, where did you reside?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I resided in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And during that school year, sir, specifically from April 30th through the end of the school year, which I believe is, what?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of the school year was in late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, did you, sir, as a teacher, from April 30th through the end of the school year, did you have colleagues who were working at the school who were of the ethnic background known as Bosniak Muslims, with all due respect?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I socialised with people regardless of their ethnic background. I socialised with Bosniaks, Bosnian Muslims. I had colleagues, workmates, Azedin Oklopcic. He was a teacher of history and geography. Said Mesanovic was there, too. He taught physics and maths. Enver Alagic who taught physical education. We were all friends, and the feeling was always mutual.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During the time period, sir, of April --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During the time period of April 30th, 1992, up through and including an incident at Hambarine of May 22nd, 1992, do you have a recollection, sir, that your colleagues that you've just mentioned continued to work on a regular and daily basis at the school?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they came regularly, day in, day out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Likewise, sir, we understand from the testimony that was led by the OTP and some from the Defence, that the tensions were high during the spring and summer of 1992 in the Prijedor Municipality among the various ethnic groups. Did you experience at any time during the summer and spring of 1992 any parents sharing their views in connection with safety and security of their children at the schools who were not of the Serb ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Where I used to work, there were Croatian children, too. And of course, parents would come to see me. They would come worried about their children. I told them there was no need for them to worry, that I will guard their children against harm just as I would guard my own. Because children, for me, are the most important thing, just like a doctor must take the oath of Hippocrates, so it was my, even if unprescribed, duty and oath as a teacher that children were what matter the most. Children are not born Croats, Muslims, or Serbs. A child is a child. And for me, a child is always sacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Regardless of their ethnic background. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did at any time, sir, during your personal observations of Dr. Stakic's family, specifically his parents and his wife, did you ever determine whether or not they held any prejudices or had feelings of discriminatory nature against non-Serbs, Bosniak Muslims and Croatians?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single word, not a single gesture would have led me to believe anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic, having known him in his youth, raised by his parents to be a purist and promote some sort of Serbian -- pure Serbian identity?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was raised, and that was also what I later taught him, to love all people regardless of their skin colour, regardless of their ethnic background. He was taught to respect all the good people and to steer clear of all evil people. Because there are evil people everywhere. In every ethnic group, you have evil people. Fortunately, however, there is still a good number of good people around, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you have an opinion, sir, with respect to Dr. Stakic as to whether he loved all people regardless of their skin colour, regardless of their ethnic background, and treated them fairly and decently throughout the period of time that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could compare this to building a house. When you build a house, first you lay the foundations. If the foundations are solid, then for a long time, you won't need to do any mending on the house. What I wish to say is that the foundations of a good, proper upbringing are with the family and with the school. And you can see the results of this quality upbringing with Dr. Stakic even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'd like to ask a final open-ended question, if I may. Is there anything, sir, else at this time that you would like to share with us with respect to Dr. Stakic, his personality, reputation, and character?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said whatever I wanted to say, and I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 12.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the fact that the witness is not in the courtroom, I take it that there is any request by one of the parties? Or otherwise, the witness should be brought in immediately. Thank you. Mr. Makovski, may I ask you to answer now the questions put to you by the Prosecution in the same decent and concrete way as you did before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Makovski, thank you, sir, for coming to The Hague and for enlightening us with your knowledge of Dr. Stakic's childhood and upbringing and what you know about his life. I'm going to try in the interests of being as efficient as possible with the limited time we have this week to ask you very direct questions and I appreciate you trying to give me as concrete an answer as possible. As I, you told us you taught Dr. Stakic his alphabet. Can you tell us what grades you were teaching when Dr. Stakic was your pupil.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first, second, and third grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you were his teacher for those three grades. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you testified that after Dr. Stakic moved away for his schooling, I believe, and went to higher grades, you saw him again in 1992 in a restaurant called Oskar or Pale. Is it correct that the restaurant had changed his name from Oskar to Pale?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The restaurant's name was Oskar, but the man who runs it and owns it, the man's name was Pale. And that's what people to used to call the restaurant, Pale's. But actually the official name of the restaurant is Oskar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand you were excited about seeing Dr. Stakic on that occasion. Did you happen to notice who the other individuals were? You said there were five or six individuals with him. Did you notice or recognise any of those people?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I wasn't looking. I wasn't interested. I was only interested in Dr. Stakic coming forward and rushing towards me, and even if he had been surrounded by a hundred thousand of other people, I wouldn't have seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I gather from your testimony that you believe you know Dr. Stakic well. You know him well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about his life, and perhaps you can enlighten us about some areas, that you can provide further information. First, before I begin, were you a member of any political party following the -- during or following the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party since 1994. In that year, there was a possibility that I would become the principal of the school, and no person who was not a member of a party could be the principal. That is why I became a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, although I'm not a Serb. I had no problem with becoming a member. However, as I've already pointed out, in 1994, I became very ill and developed a heart condition. Dr. Stakic practically saved my life. So I couldn't become the principal of the school because my illness got in the way. But that was the sole and only reason why I joined the party, and that was the only time I ever set foot in those offices, and never again after that. Nor did I ever attend any of the party's meetings, the meetings of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That answer is helpful to us. Sir, can you tell us, then, in 1990, were you living in the area of Maricka in the surroundings of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this whole time ever since 1950, I have been residing in the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did your work or your friendships cause you to travel often to the area of Omarska? Were you familiar with what was going on in the area of Omarska and Maricka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't travel to Maricka during that period. I worked there between 1968 and 1975. In 1972 -- in 1971 and 1972, I wasn't working there because I was doing my regular military service with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the period of time you were referring to, I worked in Busnovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that concrete answer. Sir, do you know what Dr. Stakic's medical specialty was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us about Dr. Stakic's political life? Do you know if he was active in any political parties, and when he became active in those parties?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never liked politics. My -- I was always particularly fond of music, sports, and fishing. I never knew much about politics, I never really followed politics. I only knew enough to know who the president of the municipality was, who the mayor was. But the rest of it, I wasn't interested in at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you were unaware of Dr. Stakic's political positions, his activities in political parties, and his political views. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, we talked about the period of 1992, and you told us that because of electricity, it was difficult to follow the media. But did you -- perhaps you had a radio with batteries or read Kozarski Vjesnik. Did you see any interviews or discussions in the media regarding Dr. Stakic during the period from the takeover of the municipality on the 30th of April, 1992, let's say, through the end of that year?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a radio with batteries. And I wasn't buying Kozarski Vjesnik, the newspaper. So I had no idea really about political life and what was going on, or about Dr. Stakic's work in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that very concrete answer. Sir, can you tell us when Dr. Stakic returned as the president of the municipality of Prijedor? Are you aware that he was the president for two different periods of time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that very precise answer. Sir, did you hear about the attempts to arrest Simo Drljaca and the arrest of Dr. Kovacevic in Prijedor in, I believe it was 1996 or 1997? I believe it was 1997.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Dr. Kovacevic also through the media and also of Simo Drljaca, who was arrested as far as I can remember, that is, there was an armed conflict as a result of which he was killed. Jezero Gradina. I heard this in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your knowledge of Dr. Stakic's character, what you knew of him as a child, was he a person who would run away from a false accusation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a sincere person. He would never run away from false accusations, and he would never tell a lie. I'm absolutely convinced of that. As a boy, he was always outspoken, sincere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of the fact that in 1997, after the attempt to arrest Mr. Drljaca, that Dr. Stakic, who was then the president of the municipality, fled Prijedor and went into hiding?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the record, if I may, just object to the form of the question and we would like to have -- if the OTP could provide us with that information since they are putting it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that following the attempt to arrest Mr. Drljaca, and following the arrest of Mr. Kovacevic, Dr. Stakic left his position in Prijedor? And it wasn't until 19 - excuse me - 2001 that he was arrested and found in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he had left Prijedor, but I don't know where he went to, whether he had fled, whether he just left of his own accord. I couldn't say really. I only know that he did leave. Where he went to eventually, I don't know, and I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to present Exhibit S2 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please put it on the ELMO directly. Can you identify, Mr. Makovski, what is depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see very clearly. I can only this line saying "Prijedor." Can you zoom in a little bit, please. Fine. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and tell us where, at that time when you lived in Prijedor, where did you reside? Could you point it? You have a pointer.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me take a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please indicate it on the ELMO at the --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's near --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Yes, there we can follow what you are indicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just suggest, there is a bigger map, if Your Honour is interested. S2-1. The same map is blown up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, it may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is too small for me to see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When using now S2-1, could you please focus on the centre and put it on the ELMO and focus on the centre of Prijedor. Can you now identify your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. This is my street, Savo Kovacevic Street. And then I think it's here, this, this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't see the coordinates from here that we can describe it for the purposes of the transcript. Does the Prosecution have the same map that we can see? No. What would be the next important building?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The blue skyscraper. And near the blue one is the red one. You may have heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do believe the street names appear, if someone with extremely good eyesight tries to read those. Perhaps the usher might be able to read them. I can't, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we know where we are. I think for the purposes of transcript, this is enough. What was the distance from your building to the building of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So approximately the same distance to the building of the SUP -- MUP, the police?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's all nearby. You just have to cross the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand, it's unfortunate for us that we don't have actually the possibility to visit the town of Prijedor. We would really like to do so, but at the moment it seems not to be possible at all. Therefore, we need your assistance, and we are extremely grateful for this assistance. I took it from your testimony of yesterday that apparently you never visited Dr. Stakic in his -- at that time when he worked in the municipal building, that you never visited him there in his capacity as such. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you been ever in 1992, for other reasons, been in this -- in one of these two buildings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been to the SUP building to ask for a permit. At that time, you couldn't move about, about the town, the streets of Prijedor, without a special authorisation. As I've already told you, I had a property at Kozara, in Malo Palanciste. I used to go there quite often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the reason that you needed such a permit, and when did it start that you needed this permit?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I simply needed to have it because you were not allowed for security reasons to move about after the attack on Prijedor. I got the authorisation after about 10 to 15 days following the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have to queue up in the building or in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My friend's sister worked for the MUP, ministry of the interior. So it was easy for me to obtain this authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see, either in front of the building of the Municipal Assembly or of the police, people lining up there, queuing up?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said "at that time." Sometime later or earlier?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about the period preceding that time. I didn't see anything. And later, if you want to know -- do you want to know before the war, during the war, or after the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should concentrate on 1992, and here specifically --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Tell me, where was the school building located?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me what exactly you mean. The school where I worked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The school where you worked, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see it on this map, not my school. My school is 20 kilometres away from -- 20 kilometres outside the town of Prijedor to the southeast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which direction? Could you name a village or hamlet in which direction it was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can specify exactly how you get there. You go -- you take the road to Celpak, and then from Celpak to a hamlet called Gomjenica. And then you follow the road to Cela, and then on to Sanicani where the fish pond is. And then to Rakelici, Knezevici, Kovac, Busnovi, and then the last stop is Kondici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this clear information. Whenever you took this route, were you ever stopped by control posts, or did you have free access on the road during the entire period, during the entire year of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no checkpoints along that particular road. And anyone was free to move about that particular part of Prijedor Municipality. There were no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this permit you mentioned before, you needed only to visit your farm? May we call it farm. But not a special permit for taking the daily route to school. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you often pass by the building of the Municipal Assembly or the police office?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time. I would go to the bus stop; and from there, by bus, I would go to school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming now to this meeting in mid-July 1992 in the restaurant Oskar, apparently the owner named Pale, would it -- could we see this on the map you have before you, where it's located? For the purposes of the transcript, once again, could you assist us -- can you identify the name of the road. Unfortunately, my glasses are not good enough to read this.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately here, in the vicinity of the new hospital, about a hundred metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How far is it from there to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been at the Keraterm building?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
