utterances.text: Did you pass by? It seems to be not that far for example, from this restaurant, looking on the map.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is Keraterm? The vicinity of which other building? Then I shall perhaps be able to tell you immediately how far it is from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can see Cirkin Polje, first of all. That's right. And then can you find yourself Keraterm building? Otherwise we for these purposes should use S2.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the usher please be so kind and put S2 on the ELMO. And please, zoom a little bit. Yes, stop. Thank you. Can you see now the building where one can read "Keraterm."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever pass this area, by car or...?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I never went there. I only took the road towards Malo Palanciste, and this location, Keraterm, I don't know where it is. I've heard of a place that was something like a collection centre there. But believe me, I never passed that way; I never paid any attention to that. I can now see that this is in Prijedor, but I don't know what building it is. Is that the brickyard building or something else? I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it your testimony under solemn declaration that you never heard that -- or did you hear whether or not people were brought to Keraterm in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of Keraterm. I heard that there were collection centres there for people who were supposed to leave and go somewhere else. That is all I know and all I ever heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know about other such centres, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm also familiar with the name of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about Omarska?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have also heard of Omarska. That was later on. And I also later on heard about the barracks located in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So these four areas or buildings were used for the same purpose from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I've heard. Believe me, I didn't see any of them. I only heard. How credible that is, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I would tell you that the predecessor of Dr. Stakic was brought to one of these, as you call it, centres and later on disappeared? Nobody knows about his fate. We heard his spouse telling us that she don't want to believe that he was killed; she still hopes that he's alive. So therefore, we have to take it in the moment that he just disappeared, the one being and exercising the same function as Dr. Stakic immediately before the takeover. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to this meeting, mid-July 1992, how long did it take approximately? Ten minutes, an hour?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five minutes approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us it was a group of about 5, 6 persons. Were some of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, even if there had been a lot more people, I wouldn't have noticed anybody but Miso. I didn't see anybody. I didn't see how they were dressed. I don't have -- I'm not that observant in any case. For example, my wife will sometimes hold it against me and will get angry if I didn't notice that she has bought something new and she has put something new on, a new piece of clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Happens apparently in many families. But coming back to this discussion, you expressed, if I take the -- your entire description of the development of Dr. Stakic, I take it that to a certain extent, you were disappeared that he didn't continue with his career as a physician. Did you express your disappointment also vis-a-vis Dr. Stakic at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, we just exchanged a few conventional phrases such as "how are you," "how's life," "how have you been doing." The words that are exchanged between a couple of friends who don't have a lot of time for in-depth conversations. That was a brief meeting, but a pleasant one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let me come to the second meeting. No doubt that it was focussed on your health problems. But did you at that point in time discuss with Dr. Stakic, because this is of extreme importance for us to know, what brings a physician to the decision to act in the political area? Did you discuss this with your good friend, Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for a single moment. I told you, I don't like politics. I don't even like discussing politics. I'm sure you are aware of what politics did to us. That's why I don't ever again want to hear the word "politics," let alone discuss it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can totally understand this view. Nevertheless, I have to ask you, did you know if, and in case yes, when Dr. Stakic was no longer president of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But an approximation, was it before 1994?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Between 1992 and 1994, I didn't see him. I only saw him in 1994 when he was already the head of the occupational medicine department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you didn't take the opportunity to discuss with him "now I'm satisfied again you're in the right job and departing from politics"? Did you exchange words on this issue, what I believe would be normal among friends?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our conversation focussed on my condition. The diagnosis was angina pectoris stabilis. My life was at stake. We didn't have time for other things. We didn't, therefore, discuss anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Some minutes ago, transcript page 59, line 13 to 14, you stated: "I only knew enough to know who the president of the municipality was, who the mayor was." Who were these persons, president of the municipality, mayor?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew that in 1992, Miso was the president of the municipality. And later on, I didn't know who the president of the municipality was because the whirlwind of the war was raging. And I focussed on my family, myself, and my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I quoted that -- from the transcript is reads "the president of the municipality" and the "mayor." Is it the same for you, or are these two difference persons?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the specific case of Prijedor, currently, there's the president of the municipality, Mr. Murselovic, and the mayor of Prijedor, Mrs. Nada Sevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about 1992? Apparently from this quote, it reads "I only knew enough in 1992." Were these two different positions, one president of the municipality and the other the mayor, or was it the same position, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in 1992, the two were the same because only recently in Prijedor I've heard there were two positions, the president of the municipality, and the mayor of the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question: Were you ever aware that during the year 1992, one or several of your colleagues suddenly disappeared, no longer appeared at work, and later on nobody knew about their fate?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school year 1992 ended. It was the end of May. And the next school year began in October 1992. I've already stated that in my school, the -- there was a huge fluctuation of staff. There was a huge turnover of staff. So people would come, stay for half a year or so; and then whenever they found a better job, a job closer to their place of residence, they would leave. There were a number of colleagues, Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks whom I knew only for a short period of time. They would come and go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of one of your colleagues, be it concrete in your school or in other schools, being detained in one of the four facilities you mentioned yourself previously?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Makovski, am I right interpreting the meaning of the first name of Dr. Stakic as a person who is nice to the world?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: In some newspapers, and by some witnesses, Dr. Stakic was described as a polite, quiet, and calm person who is in control of his feelings. And at the same time, as a resolute and determined man. Do you agree with this assessment of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Then, in that regard, does Dr. Stakic resemble you a person who would allow somebody to manipulate himself?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he wouldn't, but people involved in politics will do all sorts of things which may appear sincere and honest. However, when one looks deeper, one will find only lies. And if he had believed other people's words, the words of the people who actually lied to him, then he may have been manipulated by people who would present their lies as truths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. One more question. How can you explain that Dr. Stakic, being clever, intelligent, decent, peaceful, and nonviolent person, agreed to become the president of Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff in the situation when it was apparently clear that violence is imminent and unavoidable?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you are asking me. If you have asked me why he accepted to be the president of the municipality, then I would be able to answer your question. But I'm not aware of any Crisis Staff. This is a completely new term for me. If your question regards the function of the president of the municipality, I can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Are you aware now that Dr. Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So my last question: Today, you told at transcript page 49, line 6, that you did find Dr. Stakic smiling, happy, and joyful, in July of 1992. It was known that it was time when Dr. Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff. And when after the use of armed force against non-Serbian population, detention camps were created, and forceful removal of the non-Serb population in Prijedor municipality started. How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow that this may be true, but believe me when I say I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I have a couple of questions, very short, I hope. You told us that you had a special permit to travel to your -- I don't know, as a house or place in the mountains or in the fields. And then you didn't need a permit to go to your school every day. The question is why the difference?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My journey to school took me mostly through Serbian villages. Only Cela was predominantly Bosniak, so there were no problems there. Whereas my property on Mount Kozara is on the opposite side. And I had to pass through the entire town. And only then would I reach my property. For safety reasons, one needed a permit in order to move through the town. The permit obligation applied to everybody, not only to me who is not a Serb, but also to others, to Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I understood that. But the question is, then, it depended on the road you should take at that time that you were needing a permit. And the road you took to the mountains was to the northeast, I suppose, of the town of Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Northwest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Northwest, okay.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're correct. Northeast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Then if you wanted to go, let's say, southwest where there are a lot of villages that we were informed were mostly from Croatian ethnicity, you needed a permit also?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never went there. I assume that you're talking about the area towards Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went there. I mostly went to my workplace. My wife is also from that area. And I really didn't have any need to go to other areas or other parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: No colleagues of you had commented on that sort of things, for instance, going to school, I mean? Some colleagues of you might come from Prijedor also and might not have needed a permit to go to school. But then they could go other places; it is not necessary for you to have been there. Have you heard about a permit being required to go to Ljubija? And I'm sorry for the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. These passes were issued once the school was already over. It was in June. Some 10 or 15 days after the attack on Prijedor. These passes were valid for some ten days or so, and then they were discontinued. The passes were in place for a short period of time until the situation in the town was again calm and restored back to order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was approximately around the 10th or 15th of June 1992, up to the 25th of June, 1992. Within that period, the schools didn't work, so my colleagues did not come to school. They didn't need to go to school. I went to school because my wife, my wife's parents and relatives live near that school. So I would go to visit them. At the same time, I had that property on Mount Kozara, and I needed the permit to go there. But it was a mere formality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, yes we have two areas we would like to question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I should probably check with the Court on this first one, it's regarding the indictment. It was a question that was raised by Mr. Koumjian. So I would like to ask this witness specifically a question relating to the indictment in March of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a couple of questions by the Prosecutor in connection with Dr. Stakic leaving Prijedor and Dr. Stakic being arrested in March or thereabouts of 2001. Are you aware, sir, since it's public knowledge, that the indictment against Dr. Stakic was always, throughout the period including that that they arrested the late Dr. Milan Kovacevic, confidential, sealed and not disclosed to the public, that no one knew that there was an indictment against Dr. Stakic? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will just change the topic if you will for a second. The Honourable Judge Vassylenko asked you a question. I just want to be clear on it, and if permitted by the Court, to ask a follow-up question, relating specifically to page 73, and the Court's reference to page 49, if I may. Sir, you were asked a question on when you saw Dr. Stakic in the restaurant in July of 1992 and you described him as being, as the records reflects by the Court, as being happy, joyful, and smiling. Am I correct to understand, sir, that Dr. Stakic was happy, joyful, and smiling as to the general situation in the Prijedor Municipality, or was he happy, joyful, and smiling once he recognised, approached, and embraced you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I too, was happy and joyful and so was he. Because after a long period of time, we met. That was the reason for his joy. I don't know what else was there for him to be particularly joyous about. He was not a drunkard. He never smoked. He was really very happy and joyous for precisely that reason, because he met me. He shouted out with joy, "here's my old teacher."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll try to make it just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, forgive me if I'm not looking you in the eye. But it's okay, it's just for one question. Sir, you indicated that you had no knowledge about what was going on or even that these camps existed in Omarska in 1992. The Omarska, the Keraterm camps, and this Trnopolje camp. And you told us yesterday that you consider yourself a Yugoslav, that it was a beautiful country. And I presume that there were many people like you, including your Serb neighbours, who felt no discrimination against other ethnicities and would never have supported a government if they had known that they were putting thousands of people, your fellow citizens, from Prijedor in camps where they were tortured and many killed. Would you agree that the good people of Prijedor, including the Serb population, would not have tolerated that had they known the truth?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that those people that deceived the people of Prijedor about these camps, that they helped perpetuate this persecution of your Muslim and Croat neighbours?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MAKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether this was the case. I take it that this was possible, but personally, I don't know, believe me, please. I don't know the truth. And if I knew the truth, I would tell you. Above all, I love people, no matter who they were. I don't like to see anyone suffering because no man is born to suffer. We're all born to live our lives because we only have one life. There's no spare life to use. And that is why all those who are suffering -- that is why all those who are subjecting to other people to suffering must be persecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no other questions. The last issue to be resolved is the question of the visit. Apparently, it was your wish to see and meet Dr. Stakic. Before we can rule on this, please be advised that we learned from both Detention Unit and security here that it is in the interests of security preferable to have a visit in the Detention Unit. Two prerequisites, we would need the consent of Dr. Stakic that he wants to receive the visit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I fully agree to receive this visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you, do you as well agree and want to visit Dr. Stakic in the United Nations Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I would like to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After conferring, the Trial Chamber decides, and having heard no objections by the side -- from the side of the Prosecution, that we give our consent to a visit in the Detention Unit. All the other prerequisites have to be decided by the responsible persons in the Detention Unit and within the framework of OLAD. So the formal prerequisites from our point of view and from our side are met. It remains for me to thank you, not only for coming, but also for testifying here. And I hope that it will be possible for you to bring the message to your neighbours and to the younger ones in Prijedor that it is the mandate of this Tribunal to find the truth. There is not one truth; we are aware of this. We have to come as close as possible to this, and we try our very best. And therefore, also others should be encouraged to do the same as you did, to come here and to testify, whatever their religion or ethnicity may be. And it would be extremely helpful if that what is brought as a message to Prijedor is not only the one side of the coin, but also to try to get access to that what is told to us by numerous witnesses, leaving for a moment aside the personal responsibility of the one or other person. But there can be no reasonable doubt at all that these killings, torture, persecution, crimes against humanity happened in your town, in your municipality. And I hope that this will be also included in the lessons in the schools your younger colleagues, and I hope this will be also your message when coming home to Prijedor. And we wish you a safe return. You're excused for the day. This concludes today's hearing. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00, in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
